# A Near-Optimal Offline Algorithm for Dynamic All-Pairs Shortest Paths in Planar Digraphs

Debarati Das<sup>∗</sup> Maximilian Probst Gutenberg<sup>†</sup> Christian Wulff-Nilsen<sup>‡</sup>

**Abstract**

In the planar, dynamic All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) problem, a planar, weighted digraph _G_ undergoes a sequence of edge weight updates and the goal is to maintain a data structure on _G_, that can quickly answer distance queries between any two vertices \(x,y\in V(G)\).

The currently best algorithms [FOCS’01, SODA’05] for this problem require \(\tilde{O}(n^{2/3})\) worst- case update and query time, while conditional lower bounds [FOCS’16] show that either update or query time \(\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})\) is needed<sup>1</sup>.

In this article, we present the first algorithm with near-optimal \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})\) worst-case update and query time for the offline setting, where the update sequence is given initially. This result is obtained by giving the first offline dynamic algorithm for maintaining dense distance graphs (DDGs) faster than recomputing from scratch after each update.

Further, we also present an _online_ algorithm for the incremental APSP problem with \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})\) worst-case update/ query time. This allows us to reduce the online dynamic APSP problem to the online decremental APSP problem, which constitutes partial progress even for the online version of this notorious problem.

## 1 Introduction

In the planar, dynamic All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) problem, one is given a planar, directed and weighted graph _G_=(_V,E,w_) undergoing edge updates, i.e. edge insertions and deletions and the goal is to maintain a data structure that processes edge updates and can return for any pair of vertices \(x,y\in V\) , the distance _d<sub>G</sub>(x,y_) from _x_ to _y_ in the current version of _G_. In this work we use a somewhat restricted setting where the embedding is preserved throughout. Thus the allowed updates are edge weight increases and decreases.

This problem is maybe the most notorious open problem in planar dynamic graph algorithms: while a data structure exists \[16, 25\] that achieves worst-case update and query time \(\tilde{O}(n^{2/3})\) and a conditional lower bound \[1\] indicates that \(\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})\) update and query time is essentially necessary, progress to close this gap has proven elusive.

**Research Question 1.** _Can we close the gap between_ \(\tilde{O}(n^{2/3})\) _and_ \(\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})\) _update and query time for planar, dynamic APSP?_

Currently all approaches to achieve fast update and query times boil down to rather straightforward extensions of static algorithms combined with the simple fact that there exists an _r_-division for any planar graph. Our approach involves a recursive decomposition into _r_-divisions.

**Definition 1.1** (r-division)**.** _Given planar embedded graph G and_ \(r\ge 1\)_, an r-division is a set of O(n/r_) _edge-induced subgraphs G_<sub>1</sub>=_G_\[_E_<sub>1</sub>\]_,G_<sub>2</sub>=_G_\[_E_<sub>2</sub>\]_,...,G<sub>k</sub>=G_\[_E<sub>k</sub>_\]_, called_ pieces_, each of vertex size at most r where E_<sub>1</sub>_,E_<sub>2</sub>_,...,E<sub>k</sub> partition the edge set E, such that each piece G<sub>i</sub> shares at most_ \(O(\sqrt{r})\) _vertices_ \(\partial G_i\) _with any of the other pieces. Further all vertices_ \(\partial G_i\) _are on a constant number of holes of G<sub>i</sub> (where a_ hole _of G<sub>i</sub> is a face in the induced graph G<sub>i</sub> that is not a face of G)._

For convenience, we will assume the vertices of the _O_(1) holes of a piece _P_ are exactly the boundary vertices of _P_. This can always be ensured by adding, for each hole _h_, infinite-weight dummy edges between boundary vertices of _h_ that are consecutive in the cyclic ordering of the vertices of _h_.

**Definition 1.2** (Capped Recursive decomposition)**.** _Given graph G and_ \(r\ge 1\)_, an r_-capped recursive decomposition _of G is a forest_ R _with_ \(\lfloor lrr\rfloor\) _levels where each node is associated with a subgraph of G. In particular, each child node is associated with a subgraph of the graph associated with its parent node. Further, the nodes in_ R _that are at distance i from the root, form an r/_2_<sup>i</sup>-division of G (and an r/_2_<sup>i</sup>-division of their parent’s graph) and leaf nodes consist of a single edge only. We often do not distinguish between a node and its associated subgraph of G._

It is well-known that such an _r_-capped recursive decomposition can be found for any _r_ and planar _G_ in linear time \[26\]. The approach of \[16, 25\] is to initially construct an _n_<sup>2/3</sup>-capped recursive decomposition R, where for each subgraph _H_ in R, it computes the distances \(\partial H\times\partial H\) which are stored as a complete graph over \(\partial H\) (so-called _dense distance graph (DDG)_ of _H_), and finally exploit a clever modification of Dijkstra’s algorithm (see the Theorem below) to implement queries in \(\tilde{O}(n^{2/3})\) time by leveraging the DDGs.

**Theorem 1.3** (FR-Dijkstra, see \[16, 21\])**.** _Given a graph G, and r-capped recursive decomposition_ R _and dense distance graphs for every graph in_ R_. Then, there exists an algorithm that for any_ \(x,y\in V\)_, computes the distance d<sub>G</sub>(x,y_) _in time_ \(\tilde{O}(n/\sqrt{r})\).

Both \[16, 25\] give a (static) algorithm to compute for a given graph _H_ that is associated with a root in R, the DDG for every \(H'\) in R with \(H'\subseteq H\) in total time \(\tilde{O}(r)\); since there are _O(n/r_) pieces _H_, the total preprocessing time is thus \(\tilde{O}(n)\). Further, after an edge weight change to _G_, the algorithm only has to locate the affected root graph _H_ containing the edge, and one can simply recompute the dense distances graphs in the tree rooted at _H_ from scratch, again in \(\tilde{O}(r)\) time.

Thus, previous APSP algorithms maintained the DDGs of the pieces essentially by applying a static algorithm at every update step and obtained a dynamic APSP algorithm rather using the _r_-divisions technique in planar graphs. We ask whether there is a way of maintaining DDGs that does not require recomputation from scratch but rather maintains them dynamically. More concretely, we pose the following question.

**Research Question 2.** _Can a DDG be maintained dynamically with sublinear update time (and small query time)?_

We note that so far, the question about whether there exists an efficient encoding of DDG that can be maintained during updates with only a small number of bits changed over each update is not known either. In particular, for any DDG over an _n_-vertex graph _G_, there is no known encoding that does not have to change \(\Omega(n)\) bits on average for each update.

## 2 Contributions

In this article, we present the first partial progress on this long-standing problem. We give the first algorithm that achieves the desired update/query time in the offline setting<sup>2</sup>. Moreover, if the graph is _incremental_, i.e. the update sequence only consists of edge weight decreases, the data structure works in the online setting. Due to the lower bound of Abboud and Dahlgaard \[1\] that extends for both offline and online incremental setting, our bounds are tight up to polylogarithmic factor.

**Theorem 2.1.** _\[Near-Optimal Dynamic APSP\] There exists a data structure for the planar, dynamic APSP problem in the offline setting, i.e. where the update sequence is accessible from the beginning of the algorithm, that has worst-case update time and query time_ \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})\) _and preprocessing time_ \(\tilde{O}(n)\)_. The data structure is deterministic._

_If the graph is incremental then our data structure works in the online setting._

**Remark 2.2.** _More generally, for any_ \(\delta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]\)_, we obtain an offline dynamic APSP data structure with worst-case update time_ \(\tilde{O}(n^\delta)\) _and query time_ \(\tilde{O}(n^{1-\delta})\)_. By the lower bound by Abboud and Dahlgaard \[1\] which extends to the offline setting, this is tight for all choices of_ \(\delta\)_. Further, we improve for every constant_ \(\delta\in(0,\frac{1}{2}]\) _on the previous state-of-the-art._

Even more interestingly, we achieve our result by designing a new algorithm that efficiently maintains DDGs. We remind the reader that so far, even maintaining an encoding undergoing a sublinear number of changes in _n_ was not known.

**Theorem 2.3.** _Given a planar embedded graph G along with an r-capped recursive division_ R _of G, there exists a data structure that maintains the DDG of every node H in_ R _in the offline_<tbc>

<sup>2</sup>Here, we only assume that the update sequence is offline, i.e. is initially presented the data structure, while queries can be online.

<tbc>_setting, such that each update is processed in_ \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{r})\) _worst-case update time, and the weight of each edge_ (_x,y_) _with_ \(x,y\in\partial H\) _can be returned in query time O_(log_n). Moreover the data structure is deterministic and has a preprocessing time_ \(\tilde{O}(n)\).

_If the graph is incremental, then our data structure also works in the online setting._

It is not hard to see from the discussion above how this result can be combined with Theorem 1.3 to derive Theorem 2.1 as a corollary. Thus, the following sections are concerned with proving Theorem 2.3.

Our result can be applied to obtain an improvement to the following variant of dynamic max flow/min st-cut:

**Corollary 2.4.** _Given an n-vertex undirected planar flow network G with edge capacities, a source s, and a sink t, there is a deterministic data structure that can maintain the value of a max flow from s to t (equivalently, the value of a min st-cut) under either an offline sequence of edge weight changes or an online sequence of edge weight decreases. Each update and each query for the current max flow value can be handled in_ \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})\) _worst-case time._

The previous best update/query time bound was \(\tilde{O}(n^{2/3})\) by Italiano et al.\[20\]. Corollary 2.4 follows easily by replacing the trivial dynamic DDG algorithm in \[20\] with our data structure; the proof can be found in Appendix E.

### Conceptual Contribution.

We believe that our techniques and conceptual ideas give first indications towards designing such algorithms in the online setting:

• Our main conceptual change is a shift in perspective to view DDGs as a data structure and allow for small (but non-constant) query times. This is in stark contrast to previous literature where the DDGs where mostly seen as complete graphs that where explicitly constructed.<tbc>

• Further, our online incremental DDG data structure can be used to reduce the online dynamic APSP problem to the online decremental DDG setting. More precisely, if one can give an online algorithm A that maintains a DDG on a graph subject to edge weight increases with worst-case update time \(\tilde{O}(n^{1-\epsilon})\) for any \(\epsilon>0\), query time \(\tilde{O}(1)\), and preprocessing \(\tilde{O}(n)\), then there exists an online algorithm B for the dynamic APSP problem with worst-case update/query time \(n^{2/3-\Omega(\epsilon)}\). A precise statement and proof can be found in Section D.

## 3 Related Work

### Dynamic Shortest Paths in Planar Graphs.

As stated in the introduction, the only two dynamic data structures for APSP in planar graphs are currently \[16, 25\]. Both achieve update time \(\tilde{O}(n^\delta)\) and query time \(\tilde{O}(n^{1-\delta/2})\) for \(\delta\in[0,1]\). In particular, for \(\delta=\frac{2}{3}\), they achieve update and query time \(\tilde{O}(n^{2/3})\). We note that various improvements followed that improved the above algorithms by logarithmic or doubly-logarithmic terms or generalized the result \[29, 21, 18\].

A lower bound for the exact problem, given in \[1\], stipulates that \(\tilde{\Omega}(n^\delta)\) update time and \(\tilde{\Omega}(n^{1-\delta})\) query time is necessary if one believes in the APSP conjecture.

For undirected planar graphs in the setting where one allows for a \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximation on the distance queries, Abraham, Chechik and Gavoille \[2\] presented a data structure that achieves<tbc>

<tbc>worst-case update and query time \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n}logW/\epsilon^2)\) time where _W_ is the aspect ratio of _G_. Karczmarz \[22\] achieved similar time bounds for the \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximate APSP problem for a larger family of graphs (so-called \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-separable graphs), however, the algorithm only works for _decremental graphs_. Further, the exact dynamic single-source shortest paths problem has been studied \[8\]. In very recent work by Filtser et al. \[17\], a deterministic algorithm achieving subpolynomial amortized update and query time \(n^{o(1)}/\text{poly}(\epsilon)\) was given.

### Dynamic All-Pairs Shortest Paths in General Graphs.

The dynamic exact APSP problem has received extensive attention over the past years, also in incremental and decremental settings \[4, 24, 11, 5, 12, 32, 3, 31, 15\]. However, conditional lower bounds \[1, 19\] are quite strong and, in particular, stipulate that exact APSP requires either \(\tilde{\Omega}(m)\) update or query time. This motivates the more restricted but powerful planar setting.

### Dynamic Offline Algorithms.

The purpose of studying dynamic algorithms in an offline setting is twofold. First it captures some of the inherent difficulties of the online setting, thus making any progress for the first provides significant insight towards designing an online dynamic algorithm. Secondly most of the lower bound results for standard dynamic setting also hold for offline setting. Thus, giving an efficient algorithm for the offline dynamic setting shows that no such conditional lower bound exists. Following this, substantial effort has been taken to design dynamic algorithms in offline setting. In \[9\] authors provide a fully dynamic offline algorithm that computes _O_(log<sup>4_t_</sup>_n_) approximation of all pair max flow/min cut in average \(\tilde{O}(m^{1/t+1})\) update and query time . They also propose a fully dynamic offline algorithm for all pair shortest path that computes (2_r_-1)_<sup>t</sup>_ approximation in average \(\tilde{O}(m^{1/t+1}n^{2/r})\) update and query time for \(t,r\ge 1\). \[30\] presents a fully dynamic offline algorithm computing 3 edge and vertex connectivity in an undirected graph in time _O_(log_n_) per update. \[27, 23\] studies the dynamic connectivity and reachability in graph timelines in a semi offline setting. Here the updates are given upfront while the queries can arrive online. For the connectivity problem \[23\] provides a data structure with _O(m+t_log_n_) preprocessing time and _O_(log_n_) query time. For rechability in undirected graph \[27\] gives a randomized algorithm that has _O(t_log_t_loglog_t_log_n+m_) preprocessing time and can answer all queries in _O_(log_n_loglog_t_) time.

### Static Planar Graphs.

Finally, we point out that there has been extensive work on \((1+\epsilon)\)- approximate and exact static distance oracles culminating recently in a data structure that can be constructed in _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> space and answer distance queries exactly in subpolynomial worst-case query time \[7, 28\].

## 4 Preliminaries

In this article, we assume that every graph _H_ is planar, directed and weighted with positive weights, is already embedded in the plane, is triangulated and undergoing edge weight updates given by an efficient encoding of the weight update sequence. We call a dynamic graph _H_, _incremental/ decremental_ if the weight update sequence monotonically decreases/ increases edge weights in _H_ over time. In the offline setting, we assume that the update sequence is given with the input, in<tbc>

the online setting the sequence is revealed on-the-go. We use _G_=(_V,E,w_) to denote the input graph, where _V_ is the set of vertices with _n_=|_V_|, _E_ is the set of edges and \(w:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) is the edge weight function. Assume constant time arithmetic on the weights. We let _d<sub>G</sub>(u,v_) denote the shortest path distance from _u_ to _v_ in _G_ and assume that all shortest paths at any time in _G_ are unique. This can be ensured using the deterministic perturbation technique in \[14\]).

Finally, we introduce the concept of full persistence.

**Definition 4.1** (Fully-persistent)**.** _We say a data structure undergoing an update sequence is_ fully- persistent _if every version of the data structure can be accessed and modified._

## 5 Online Incremental DDG

In this section, we show the following result which we will use in our reductions in section D and section C to get the main results of the paper.

**Theorem 5.1.** _Given input graph G, and an r-capped recursive decomposition_ R _of G with roots G_<sub>1</sub>_,G_<sub>2</sub>_,...,G<sub>k</sub>._

_Then, there exists a deterministic data structure that, given any G<sub>i</sub>, maintains the DDGs of all pieces in the tree rooted at G<sub>i</sub>. Its preprocessing time is_ \(\tilde{O}(n)\) _and it handles each edge weight decrease in G<sub>i</sub> in worst case update time_ \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{r})\)_. After every update, a query for the weight of any DDG edge of any piece in the tree rooted at G<sub>i</sub> can be answered in worst-case time_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\).

_The data structure is fully-persistent._

In our construction, we focus on the first part of the theorem statement, and only at the end of this section we show how to modify our data structure to make it persistent.

### 5.1 The Data Structure

### Preliminaries.

First, we need some additional notation. To avoid clutter, let _H=G<sub>i</sub>_. We let the updates to _H_ be encoded by tuples \(\{(e^1,\omega^1),(e^2,\omega^2),\dots\}\) where _e<sup>i</sup>_ is an edge in _H_, and \(\omega^i\) its new edge weight. In this section, we also need to argue about the embedding of _G_. We assume that we are given a combinatorial planar embedding, also often called rotation system, that specifies for each vertex _v_ in _G_, a cyclic order _e_<sub>0</sub>_,e_<sub>1</sub>_,...,e_<sub>_k_-1</sub> of the edges incident to _v_, such that in the planar embedding every _e<sub>i</sub>_ is in between _e_<sub>_i_-1</sub> and _e_<sub>_i_+1</sub>. We define a sharpest right-turn (left-turn) at _v_ from an edge _e_ to be the first out-going edge \(e'\) incident to _v_ in counter-clockwise (clockwise) order starting in _e_.

We further let for each piece _P_ (where we only talk for the rest of this section about pieces _P_ in the tree rooted at _H_), _P<sup>t</sup>_ refer the version of the piece _P_ after the first _t_ updates have been applied to _H_. In particular _P_<sup>0</sup> is the initial piece.

For each piece _P_, we let _h(P_)={_h_<sub>1</sub>(_P),h_<sub>2</sub>(_P),...,h<sub>s<sub>P</sub></sub>(P_)} be the constant number of holes such that each vertex in \(\partial P\) is on some such hole. To ease indexing and avoid clutter, we allow _h<sub>i</sub>(P_) for any positive _i_, and let it refer to the \(h_{i^\prime}(P)\) such that \(i'\) is the unique integer in \[1_,s<sub>h</sub>_\] derived from subtracting a multiple of _s<sub>h</sub>_ from _i_.

Further, for each hole \(h\in h(P)\), we let _Q(h_) denote a cyclic ordering _v_<sub>1</sub>(_h),v_<sub>2</sub>(_h),...,v<sub>s<sub>h</sub></sub>(h_) of the (boundary) vertices of _h_ such that the interior of _h_ is to the right when traversing the vertices in this order. We also abuse notation slightly and denote by \[_v<sub>i</sub>(h),v<sub>j</sub>(h_)\] for \(1\le i\le j\le s_h\) the subset {_v<sub>i</sub>(h),v_<sub>_i_+1</sub>(_h),...,v<sub>j</sub>(h_)} of _Q(h_) when the context is clear. Further, we also define a _wrapped_<tbc>

_interval_ \[_v<sub>i</sub>(h),v<sub>j</sub>(h_)\] for the hole _h_, where if \(1\le i\le j\le s_h\) the interval is defined as above and if \(1\le j<i\le s_h\), is defined to be the interval {_v<sub>i</sub>(h),v_<sub>_i_+1</sub>(_h),...,v<sub>s<sub>h</sub></sub>(h),v_<sub>1</sub>(_h),v_<sub>2</sub>(_h),...,v<sub>j</sub>(h_)}. We define (_v<sub>i</sub>,v<sub>j</sub>_) to be \[_v<sub>i</sub>,v<sub>j</sub>_\]\\{_v<sub>i</sub>,v<sub>j</sub>_}. We use the above indexing trick for _v<sub>i</sub>_’s where _i_ is potentially larger than _s<sub>h</sub>_ in conjunction with intervals, and wrapped intervals.

Finally, we require a simple data structure.

**Theorem 5.2.** _\[Last Interval Detection Data Structure\] Given a universe of size U, we can maintain a data structure that allows adding at time_ \(i\ge 1\)_, a sub-interval_ \([l_i,r_i]\subseteq[1,U]\)_, and for queries at time i where on input_ \(x\in[1,U]\)_, the data structure outputs the largest integer_ \(j\le i\)_, such that_ \(x\in[l_j,r_j]\) _where we assume that_ \[_l_<sub>0</sub>_,r_<sub>0</sub>\]=\[1_,U_\] _(so j is well-defined). If the length of the update sequence is polynomially bounded in n, then the data structure can be implemented with pre-processing time_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\) _and_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\) _worst-case update and query time._

## Initialization.

We start by computing initially, for each piece _P_ in the tree of R rooted at _H_, the DDG using the FR-Dijkstra algorithm \[16\] (we later show that we need to store slightly more information to make updates efficient). We further initialize for each piece _P_, boundary vertex \(b\in\partial P\) and for each hole \(h\in h(P)\) a Last Interval Detection data structure D_<sub>b,h</sub>_ on the universe _Q(h_)={_v_<sub>1</sub>(_h),v_<sub>2</sub>(_h),...,v<sub>s<sub>h</sub></sub>(h_)} as described in Theorem 5.2.

## Updates.

After the _t<sup>th</sup>_ update, we compute and store for each piece _P_, with \(e^t=(u^t,v^t)\in P\), the distances _d<sub>Pt</sub>(b,u<sup>t</sup>_) and _d<sub>Pt</sub>(v<sup>t</sup>,b_) for each \(b\in\partial P\). Further, for each such piece _P_, \(b\in\partial P\), and hole \(h\in h(P)\), we find the set of vertices \(S_{b,h}\subseteq Q(h)\) such that for each \(b'\in S_{b,h}\),

\(d_{P^{t-1}}(b,b')>d_{Pt}(b,u^t)+\omega^t+d_{Pt}(v^t,b').\)

We say that a vertex \(b'\in S_{b,h}\) _profits_ from _e<sup>t</sup>_.

We will later see that _S<sub>b,h</sub>_ consists of at most two subintervals of _Q(h_). We add these two subintervals to the data structure D_<sub>b,h</sub>_. Before we show how to implement updates efficiently, let us illustrate a query of the data structure.

## Queries.

Consider a query for the weight of an edge in the DDG of some piece _P_ from a boundary vertex _b_ to a boundary vertex \(b'\).

We can now simply query the data structure D_<sub>b,h</sub>_ for vertex \(b'\). This allows us to locate the last time _t_ that the shortest path from _b_ to \(b'\) (in _P_) was decreased in weight (note that technically the times of D_<sub>b,h</sub>_ and versions of the pieces _P_ do not align however it is straight-forward to pair them). Since the decrease must have resulted from decreasing the weight of edge _e<sup>t</sup>_, we can now simply output

\(d_{Pt}(b,b')=d_{Pt}(b,u^t)+\omega^t+d_{Pt}(v^t,b').\)

Since we stored _d<sub>Pt</sub>(b,u<sup>t</sup>),d<sub>Pt</sub>(v<sup>t</sup>,b_) and \(\omega^t\) at time step _t_, a look-up suffices to recover them once _t_ is known. Since \(b'\) has not profited from any edge thereafter, we conclude that the returned distances is the current distance.

## Computing Distances for Updates Efficiently.

It remains to give the precise algorithm to update the data structure when processing the _t<sup>th</sup>_ update to _H_. Here, we focus on updating a single affected piece _P_ (i.e. \(e^t\in P\)) in \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{|P|})\) time. It then follows immediately that we can update all affected pieces in time \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{r})\).

We start by describing the first step of our update procedure, that is to compute for each vertex \(x\in\partial P\), the distances _d<sub>P<sup>t</sup></sub>(x,u<sup>t</sup>_) and _d<sub>P<sup>t</sup></sub>(v<sup>t</sup>,x_). Note however, that we can find these distances in the graph _P_<sup>_t_-1</sup>, since shortest paths to _u<sup>t</sup>_ do not need to use an out-going edge of _u<sup>t</sup>_. More precisely, these distances can be found in _P<sup>t</sup>_\\{_e<sup>t</sup>_}=_P_<sup>_t_-1</sup>\\{_e<sup>t</sup>_}. An analogous observation also holds for the distances _d<sub>P<sup>t</sup></sub>(v<sup>t</sup>,x_), i.e. _d<sub>P<sup>t</sup></sub>(v<sup>t</sup>,x_)=_d_<sub>_P_<sup>_t_-1</sup></sub>(_v<sup>t</sup>,x_).

It thus remains to compute these distances in the graph _P_<sup>_t_-1</sup>. To this end, let _P_<sub>1</sub>_,P_<sub>2</sub>_,...,P<sub>k</sub>_ be the unique path in R from piece _P=P_<sub>1</sub> to the leaf piece _P<sub>k</sub>_ containing _e<sup>t</sup>_. Further, for each such _P<sub>i</sub>_, let _P_<sub>_i,_1</sub>_,P_<sub>_i,_2</sub>_,...P_<sub>_i,k<sub>i</sub>_</sub> be the siblings of _P<sub>i</sub>_ in R (this set does not contain _P<sub>i</sub>_ itself). Let <o>_P_</o><sub>_i,_1</sub>_,P_<sub>_i,_2</sub>_,...,P_<sub>_i,k<sub>i</sub>_</sub> be the dense distance graphs of all siblings of _P<sub>i</sub>_.

Next, note that \(\bigcup_{\ell,j}P_{\ell,j}^{t-1}\) forms exactly the graph _P<sup>t</sup>_\\{_e<sup>t</sup>_} by our discussion above and the fact that each leaf of R contains exactly one edge (see Definition 1.2). Further note that our data structure already holds the DDGs \(\overline{P_{i,1}^{t-1}},\overline{P_{i,2}^{t-1}},\dots,\overline{P_{i,k_i}^{t-1}}\).

Then, to find the distances _d<sub>P<sup>t</sup></sub>(v<sup>t</sup>,x_) for \(x\in\partial P\), we can invoke the following version of FR- Dijkstra which is a stronger version of Theorem 1.3.

**Theorem 5.3** (Extended FR-Dijkstra, see \[16, 21\])**.** _Given a graph G, an r-capped recursive decomposition_ R _a set of edge-disjoint pieces X_<sub>1</sub>_,X_<sub>2</sub>_,...,X<sub>k</sub> in_ R_, along with a data structure that answers queries for edge weights in their corresponding dense distance graphs_ <o>X</o><sub>1</sub>_,<o>X</o>_<sub>2</sub>_,...<o>X</o><sub>k</sub> in_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\) _time._

_Then, there exists an algorithm that given some_ \(v\in\bigcup_j\partial X_j\)_, computes a shortest path tree T<sub>v</sub> in_ \(\bigcup_j\overline{X_j}\) _in time_ \(\tilde{O}(\sum_j\sqrt{|X_j|})\).

It is not hard to see that this not only gives all distance _d<sub>P<sup>t</sup></sub>(v<sup>t</sup>,x_) when invoked for vertex _v<sup>t</sup>_, but also with a single invocation of this algorithm, we can find all distances _d<sub>P<sup>t</sup></sub>(x,u<sup>t</sup>_) by reversing all edges in the dense distance graphs and invoking the theorem again for _u<sup>t</sup>_. ## Finding _S<sub>b,h</sub>_ Efficiently.

Finally, we have to show how to compute _S<sub>b,h</sub>_ efficiently, i.e. in \(\tilde{O}(1)\) time. Similar to Lemma 5.6, we only describe how to find _S<sub>b,h</sub>_ for _b_ on a hole \(h'\neq h\). We now describe two essential sub-procedures to find _S<sub>b,h</sub>_ efficiently:

First, we need to compute the vertex \(r_{v^t,h^\prime,h}\) used in Lemma 5.6 in time \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{|P|})\) for each piece _P_ with \(h,h'\in h(P)\). We give the proof in Appendix B.1.

**Lemma 5.7.** _Given a piece P, distinct holes_ \(h,h'\in h(P)\) _and a vertex v in P. We can find the vertex_ \(r_{v,h,h^\prime}\) _in time_ \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{|P|})\).

While \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{|P|})\) seems excessive, we only need to do such a computation for each affected piece _P_ and every ordered pair of holes in _h(P_) once, so we can find all necessary vertices \(r_{v^t,h^\prime,h}\) necessary in total time \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{|P|})\).

Secondly, we require the following tool.

**Lemma 5.8.** _Given any two vertices v<sub>i</sub>(h),v<sub>j</sub>(h_) _on h, such that_ \(v_i(h),v_j(h)\unknown\in S_{b,h}\)_, there is an algorithm that in_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\) _time detects whether the edge e<sup>t</sup> is contained in the region of the plane to the right of the directed cycle consisting of the shortest path_ \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) _from b to v<sub>i</sub>(h), the path in h from v<sub>i</sub>(h_) _to v<sub>j</sub>(h_) _on h, and the reverse of the shortest path_ \(\pi_{b,v_j(h)}\) _from b to v<sub>j</sub>(h_) _(see Figure 1(b))._

Before we prove Lemma 5.8, let us show how we use these two sub-procedures to compute _S<sub>b,h</sub>_ efficiently. Here, we can employ a simple binary search strategy. Let \(r_{v^t,h^\prime,h}=v_k(h)\) in the cyclic ordering. Take two vertices \(v_i(h),v_j(h)\in Q(h)\) where _v<sub>i</sub>(h_) is the vertex preceding \(r_{v^t,h^\prime,h}\) in the cyclic ordering and \(v_j(h)=v_{i-\lfloor\frac{s_h-(k-i)}{2}\rfloor}(h)\). Recall that we can test membership of _v<sub>i</sub>(h),v<sub>j</sub>(h_) in _S<sub>b,h</sub>_ in constant time, then

• if both are in _S<sub>b,h</sub>_: we know that \([v_j(h),v_i(h)]\subseteq S_{b,h}\) and we continue the search in the interval _Q(h_)\\\[_v<sub>j</sub>(h),v<sub>i</sub>(h_)\] by setting new \(v_j(h)=v_{j-\lfloor\frac{s_h-(k-j)}{2}\rfloor}(h)\).<tbc>

• if neither of them are in _S<sub>b,h</sub>_: use Lemma 5.8 to decide whether _e<sup>t</sup>_ is in the region described in the Lemma. If so, we can conclude that \(S_{b,h}\subseteq(v_j(h),v_i(h))\) and thus repeat the same process on (_v<sub>j</sub>(h),v<sub>i</sub>(h_)) by setting new \(v_j(h)=v_{i-\lfloor\frac{i-j}{2}\rfloor}(h)\) and new _v<sub>i</sub>(h_)=_v_<sub>_i_-1</sub>(_h_); otherwise, we know that \(S_{b,h}\cap(v_i(h),v_j(h))=\emptyset\) and thus continue the search on _Q(h_)\\(_v<sub>j</sub>(h),v<sub>i</sub>(h_)). Here we set the new _v<sub>i</sub>(h_) to be the vertex following \(r_{v,h^\prime,h}\) in the cyclic ordering and \(v_j(h)=v_{j-\lfloor\frac{s_h-(k-j)}{2}\rfloor}(h)\).<tbc>

• The case where exactly one vertex is in _S<sub>b,h</sub>_ is similar. W.l.o.g assume \(v_j(h)\in S_{b,h}\). We continue the search with new \(v_i(h)=v_{i-\lfloor\frac{i-j}{2}\rfloor}(h)\) and new \(v_j(h)=v_{j-\lfloor\frac{s_h-(k-j)}{2}\rfloor}(h)\).

Thus it follows that we can do binary search in \(\tilde{O}(1)\) time using the above procedures.

## Detecting _e<sup>t</sup>_ in a Region.

It remains to prove the following Lemma.

**Lemma 5.8.** _Given any two vertices v<sub>i</sub>(h),v<sub>j</sub>(h_) _on h, such that_ \(v_i(h),v_j(h)\unknown\in S_{b,h}\)_, there is an algorithm that in_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\) _time detects whether the edge e<sup>t</sup> is contained in the region of the plane to the right of the directed cycle consisting of the shortest path_ \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) _from b to v<sub>i</sub>(h), the path in h from v<sub>i</sub>(h_) _to v<sub>j</sub>(h_) _on h, and the reverse of the shortest path_ \(\pi_{b,v_j(h)}\) _from b to v<sub>j</sub>(h_) _(see Figure 1(b))._

## Overview.

To prove the Lemma, we employ the following algorithm: first let us assume that the first edge on the shortest paths \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)},\pi_{b,v_j(h)}\) and the shortest path \(\pi_{b,v^t}\) from _b_ to _v<sup>t</sup>_ are all distinct. Here, we can use the planar embedding of _G_ to conclude whether \(\pi_{b,v^t}\) uses as a first edge an edge to the right of \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) and to the left of \(\pi_{b,v_j(h)}\) (or not) and if so we know that _e<sup>t</sup>_ is in the region; otherwise _e<sup>t</sup>_ must be outside the region.

Unfortunately, the paths \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) and \(\pi_{b,v^t}\) might share the first few (or many) edges and \(\pi_{b,v^t}\) only takes a right-turn after a while (the case where \(\pi_{b,v_j(h)}\) and \(\pi_{b,v^t}\) share many edges is analogous). We thus have to find the last vertex _x_ that is on both \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) and \(\pi_{b,v^t}\). Deciding whether \(\pi_{b,v^t}\) makes a left-turn after following \(\pi_{b,v_j(h)}\) is then again simple using the embedding. Observe that the edge _e<sup>t</sup>_ is not on \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) and \(\pi_{b,v_j(h)}\) so that we can concentrate on finding the last common vertex on the shortest paths of \(\pi_{b,u^t}\) and \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) and \(\pi_{b,v_j(h)}\), respectively.

## Storing Additional Information.

To find the vertex _x_, we need to store additional information. We use the following results.

**Theorem 5.9** (Level-Ancestor Data Structure, see \[6\])**.** _Given a tree T rooted at vertex r, there is a data structure that with preprocessing time O_(|_T_|) _and query time O_(1) _that on query for a vertex x and a positive integer d returns the d<sup>th</sup> edge on the r-to-x path in T._

We assume that on initialization of our data structure, additionally to the DDG edges, we also store for each piece \(P'\), and vertex \(b'\in\partial P'\) the shortest path out-tree \(T_{b^\prime}\) over the lower level DDGs of \(P'\), as can be computed by using Appendix B. Additionally, we know that \(T_{b^\prime}\) spans all boundary nodes of \(P'\)’s child pieces, denoted \(\partial_\text{\textit{child}}P'\). We mark these vertices in the tree and let \(T'_{b^\prime}\) be the tree derived from restricting the vertex set to \(\partial_\text{\textit{child}}P'\) (by recursively removing leaves that are not in \(\partial_\text{\textit{child}}P'\) and by contracting paths between two vertices in \(\partial_\text{\textit{child}}P'\)).

Then for each such tree, we initialize a level-ancestor data structure on \(T'_{b^\prime}\) as described in Theorem 5.9. We do the same for the in-tree \(\overleftarrow{T}_{b^\prime}\). It is not hard to observe that these computations can be done in time \(O(|T_{b^\prime}|+|\overleftarrow{T}_{b^\prime}|)=\tilde{O}(\sqrt{|P|})\) time, thus the pre-processing can still be bound by \(\tilde{O}(r)\).

After each update \((e^t,\omega^t)\), we do the same to the trees _T<sub>v<sup>t</sup></sub>_ rooted at _v<sup>t</sup>_ and the tree \(\overleftarrow{T}_{u^t}\) rooted at _u<sup>t</sup>_ computed on dense distance graphs with edge reversed. Again, this incurs at most \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{r})\) update time over all levels for each update.

## Implementing the Query Efficiently.

Now, returning to the paths \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) and \(\pi_{b,u^t}\), we distinguish two cases:

• if no edge on \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) had its weight decreased since the data structure was initialized: then we use the trees \(\overleftarrow{T}'_{v_i(h)}\) and \(\overleftarrow{T}'_{u^t}\), starting at vertex _b_, we use binary search on the parameter _d_ in the level ancestor data structures to detect which boundary vertex \(b'\) in \(\partial_childP\) is the last on the shortest paths \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) and \(\pi_{b,u^t}\) (from _b_ we use a reasonable _d_ for the paths to _v<sub>i</sub>(h_) and _u<sup>t</sup>_ respectively and if the edges agree we search the interval containing values larger than _d_ and otherwise, we search the interval containing values smaller than _d_; we repeat this step iteratively to find the last edge that is shared on the paths by recursing on the relevant subintervals; this takes at most _O_(log_n_) time).<tbc>

<tbc>Given \(b'\), let \(b''\) be the next vertex on \(\overleftarrow{T}'_{v_i(h)}[b]\) and \(b'''\) the next vertex on \(\overleftarrow{T}'_{u^t}[b]\). If \(b''\) and \(b'''\) are in different child pieces of _P_, then we can conclude that \(b'\) is equal _x_.<tbc>

<tbc>Otherwise, we know that all three vertices are incident to the child piece \(P''\). The final problem becomes to find the last common vertex of the shortest paths \(\pi_{b^\prime,b^{\prime\prime}}\) from \(b'\) to \(b''\) and \(\pi_{b^\prime,b^{\prime\prime}}\) from \(b'\) to \(b'''\).<tbc>

<tbc>It is not hard to see that this problem can now be solved by recursing on the piece \(P''\). Each binary search for the last child boundary vertex takes _O_(log_n_) time and the recursion depth is bounded by _O_(log_n_) giving a total query time of _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_n_).<tbc>

• if some edge \(e^\ell\) is the edge on \(\pi_{b,v_i(h)}\) that had last its edge weight decreased: we can then use the same strategy as suggested above on the trees \(T'_{v^\ell}\) and \(\overleftarrow{T}'_{u^\ell}\) and the edge \(e^\ell\) separately. While this increases the time to find the last child boundary vertex shared by the paths slightly, we still only require a single recursive call and therefore the query time is again _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_n_).

This completes the description of our data structure and establishes Theorem 5.1.

## Making the Data Structure Fully-Persistent.

Lastly, to turn our data structure into a fully- persistent data structure, we use the following result by \[13\].

**Definition 5.10** (Emphemeral Linked Data Structure)**.** _An_ emphemeral linked data structure _is a data structure that consists of a finite number of_ nodes _where each node has a constant number of_ words _containing either information or a pointer to another node._

**Theorem 5.11** (\[13\])**.** _Any emphemeral linked data structure, where each node has its pointer stored at a constant number of nodes at most, can be made fully-persistent at the cost of an additional_ factor _of O_(log_n_) _to the amortized/ worst-case update/ query cost._

While our described data structure is not an emphemeral linked data structure yet, we can convert multiple pointers pointing to the same node by binary trees over them which increases update times, query times and space by at most a logarithmic factor.

## A Construction of the Last Interval Detection Data Structure

Let us now show how the data structure presented in Theorem 5.2 can be constructed. We restate the theorem here for convenience.

**Theorem 5.2.** _\[Last Interval Detection Data Structure\] Given a universe of size U, we can maintain a data structure that allows adding at time_ \(i\ge 1\)_, a sub-interval_ \([l_i,r_i]\subseteq[1,U]\)_, and for queries at time i where on input_ \(x\in[1,U]\)_, the data structure outputs the largest integer_ \(j\le i\)_, such that_ \(x\in[l_j,r_j]\) _where we assume that_ \[_l_<sub>0</sub>_,r_<sub>0</sub>\]=\[1_,U_\] _(so j is well-defined). If the length of the update sequence is polynomially bounded in n, then the data structure can be implemented with pre-processing time_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\) _and_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\) _worst-case update and query time._

Assume that the length of the update sequence is bounded by _n<sup>c</sup>_ for some (possibly large) constant _c_. Our algorithm maintains at all times an incomplete binary balanced tree T with \(\lceil c\cdot log_2(n)\rceil\) levels, where the leaf nodes are the intervals that where already added in the order that they arrived in. More precisely, after time 0, T is a path of length \(\lceil c\cdot log_2(n)\rceil\) with the interval \[_l_<sub>0</sub>_,r_<sub>0</sub>\]=\[1_,U_\] as its only leaf. Every time a new interval \[_l<sub>i</sub>,r<sub>i</sub>_\] is added, we add it as a leaf to the right of interval \[_l_<sub>_i_-1</sub>_,r_<sub>_i_-1</sub>\] into T possibly creating up to _O_(log(_n_)) new internal nodes.

Now, additionally to maintaining the tree T , we maintain at each internal node _v_ of T , a dynamic interval tree (see for example \[10\]) which holds the intervals of the leaf nodes in the subtree rooted at the node. An interval tree has _O_(log_n_) update time and allows to query for any element \(x\in[1,U]\) whether there is a segment in the interval tree that contains _x_ in time _O_(log_n_). An empty interval tree can be initialized in time _O_(1).

It is not hard to see from this discussion, that on adding an interval \[_l<sub>i</sub>,r<sub>i</sub>_\] to our tree, we can maintain the data structure by creating all nodes on the leaf-to-root path from \[_l<sub>i</sub>,r<sub>i</sub>_\] to the root that are missing in T , initializing a new interval tree at them, and finally adding \[_l<sub>i</sub>,r<sub>i</sub>_\] to the interval tree of every node on the leaf-to-root path. Thus an update take worst-case update time _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_n_) time.

For a query with input _x_, we start from the root of T , then query whether _x_ is in some interval in the subtree rooted at the right child of the root. If so, we move to the right child, otherwise, we move to the left child. We repeat this procedure on the node that we moved to and do so iteratively until we navigated to a leaf. It is not hard to see that the reached leaf node is exactly the last interval that contains _x_. Since we move along a path of at most _O_(log_n_) nodes and deciding whether to go to the left or right can be decided in _O_(log_n_) time using the interval trees, we have total query time _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_n_).

This completes the proof.

## B Extending FR-Dijkstra

### B.1 Finding leftmost to rightmost shortest paths

In this section, we describe an extension to FR-Dijkstra that allows it to obtain a vertex \(r_{v,h,h^\prime}\), given a vertex v in a piece with holes _h_ and \(h'\). We will describe an extension that will not slow down FR-Dijkstra. Recall that \(r_{v,h,h^\prime}\) is found by growing a rightmost shortest path from _v_, taking the sharpest right turn at each step. After having executed FR-Dijksta to find a shortest path tree, the rightmost shortest path now is a sequence of DDG edges from the tree and we want to traverse these edges in order. At each step of the traversal, we need the cyclic ordering of outgoing tree edges that is consistent with the cyclic ordering in the underlying planar graph; this will allow us to pick the tree edge making the sharpest right turn. It thus suffices to give a preprocessing step which for each piece _P_ and each boundary vertex _u_ of _P_ computes and stores a cyclic ordering of DDG edges of _P_ outgoing from _u_. With this precomputed information, \(r_{v,h,h^\prime}\) can be found in time proportional to the shortest path tree found by FR-Dijkstra. Hence, the extension to FR-Dijkstra will not increase the overall time bound.

We may use FR-Dijkstra to precompute DDGs of all pieces bottom-up in the recursive decomposition where leaf pieces have constant size. Our preprocessing step processes pieces in the same bottom-up order. Let _P_ be a non-leaf piece _P_ and suppose that cyclic orderings have been found for all boundary vertices of all child pieces. Let _u_ be a boundary vertex of _P_. We will describe<tbc>

the preprocessing for _u_ that gives a cyclic ordering of DDG edges of _P_ outgoing from _u_. We let _h_ denote a hole of _P_ containing _u_.

Let _T_ be the shortest path tree from _u_ in _P_ found by FR-Dijkstra. This tree consists of DDG edges from child pieces of _P_. Given the precomputed cyclic orderings of these pieces, it is now fairly easy to find the ordering for _u_ in _P_. First, perform a DFS-traversal of _T_ where the next tree edge to be visited is the one that makes the sharpest right turn w.r.t. the parent tree edge; in case the parent tree edge does not exist in _T_, we regard it as a dummy edge from a vertex embedded inside _h_ to _u_. Given the precomputed information for child pieces, the DFS-traversal of _T_ can be done in _O_(|_T_|) time. The cyclic ordering of DDG edges of _P_ from _u_ is now the same as the DFS ordering of the heads of these edges.

This completes the description of the preprocessing step and we argued for its correctness. The running time is dominated by the time to compute DDGs of all pieces using FR-Dijkstra. Hence, the preprocessing step will not increase the overall time bound.

## B.2 Dealing with distinct holes

In this subsection, we give some details missing in the paper by Fakcharoenphol and Rao on how to deal with distinct holes. These details are important in our setting since we are not treating FR-Dijkstra as a black box.

Let _h_<sub>1</sub> and _h_<sub>2</sub> be two _distinct_ holes of a piece _P_ and consider a setting where FR-Dijkstra is run on some union of DDGs one of which is DDG(_P_). The issue with relaxing edges from _h_<sub>1</sub> to _h_<sub>2</sub> is that the Monge property no longer holds since _h_<sub>1</sub> and _h_<sub>2</sub> are distinct faces. We show how to extend FR-Dijkstra to handle this.

We can view the vertices of _h_<sub>2</sub> as an interval _R_ defined by starting in some arbitrary vertex and then following the cyclic ordering of _h_<sub>2</sub> until all vertices have been visited. Let _L_ be the vertices of _h_<sub>1</sub> with the cyclic ordering from _h_<sub>1</sub>. We wish to efficiently relax edges of the bipartite graph of DDG edges from _L_ to _R_.

Consider a step of FR-Dijkstra where a vertex \(u\in L\) is activated. We need to argue how to efficiently find the vertices of _R_ that get _u_ as their new parent. Clearly, these vertices induce a subpath of _h_<sub>2</sub> and hence at most two sub-intervals of _R_. Using the same procedure as in the standard FR-Dijkstra procedure, we traverse _L_ in order from _u_ until a vertex \(u'\) is found whose interval in _R_ is partially (but not fully) removed due to the activation of _u_.

FR-Dijkstra would now do binary search to determine which part of the interval of \(u'\) should belong to the interval of _u_. However, this fails since we are missing the following property: if two vertices _v_<sub>1</sub> and _v_<sub>2</sub> in _R_ have _u_ as their new parent then every vertex between them in _R_ also has _u_ as a parent.

Let _r_ be the endpoint of the rightmost DDG edge of _u_ in _P_. Split _R_ into two sub-intervals that share the endpoint _r_. Then we can in fact ensure the property above by doing binary search in each of the two sub-intervals. This follows using similar arguments to those in the proof of Lemma 5.6. Since _r_ can be obtained in constant time using the auxiliary data computed in the extension to FR-Dijkstra in Section B.1, we can thus deal with distinct holes without an asymptotic increase in the running time of FR-Dijkstra.

## C Reduction from Dynamic DDG to Incremental DDG in the Offline Setting

In this section, we give a simple reduction from the problem of maintaining a DDG on a dynamic graph to maintaining it on an incremental graph. For concreteness, we tailored the reduction to the guarantees of our incremental data structure but it is straight-forward to generalize the reduction further. From the reduction below, combined with Theorem 5.1, we immediately obtain our main Theorem 2.3 as a corollary.

**Theorem C.1.** _Given an offline data structure_ I_, that for any graph H, an r-capped recursive decomposition_ R_<sub>H</sub> of H with roots H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>, and any i, maintains the DDGs of all nodes in the tree rooted at H<sub>i</sub>, with preprocessing time_ \(\tilde{O}(r)\)_, handles each edge weight decrease affecting H<sub>i</sub> in worst-case update time_ \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{r})\) _and has query time_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\).

_Then there exists an_ offline _data structure_ F_, that given dynamic graph G along with an r- capped recursive decomposition_ R _with roots_ \(G_1,G_2,\dots,G_{k^\prime}\)_, for all j maintains the DDGs of all pieces in the tree rooted at G<sub>j</sub> with pre-processing time_ \(\tilde{O}(r)\) _and amortized update time_ \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{r})\) _and query time_ \(\tilde{O}(1)\).

_If_ I _is fully-persistent, we can turn the update and query time guarantees of_ F _into worst-case guarantees._

We prove the theorem for the root nodes \(G_1,G_2,\dots,G_{k^\prime}\). This is without loss of generality since the children of these nodes form an _r/_2-capped recursive decomposition and the data structure I can be applied to them and so on recursively, all at the cost of an additional \(\tilde{O}(1)\) factor.

In the end of this section, we argue that standard de-amortization techniques can be used to achieve worst-case update and query time. Let us now state additional preliminaries and components required by our dynamic data structure.

### Additional Notation.

We let \(\tau\) be the number of updates that _G_ is undergoing and assume \(\tau\) is a power of 2 and be polynomially bounded in _n_. We denote by _G<sup>t</sup>_=(_V,E,w<sup>t</sup>_) the graph _G after_ the _t<sup>th</sup>_ update is applied, and call each _G<sup>t</sup>_ a _version_ of _G_. In particular, _G_<sup>0</sup> is the initial graph _G_. We define a graph \(G_i^t=(V,E,\overline{w_i^t})\) for every \(0\le i\le\mathrm{lg}\tau\) and time _t_ to have the weight function defined for every \(e\in E\) by \(\overline{w_i^t}(e)=\mathrm{max}_{j\in[2^i]}w^{\lfloor t\rfloor_i+j}(e)\). We make the following straight-forward but nonetheless interesting observations.

**Observation C.2.** _For every_ \(0\le i\le\mathrm{lg}\tau\) _and time t being a multiple of_ 2_<sup>i</sup>, then for any_ \(j\in[2^i]\), \(G_{i+1}^t=G_{i+1}^{t+j}\).

## D Reduction from Dynamic DDG to Decremental DDG in the Online Setting

**Theorem D.1.** _Given an online data structure_ D_, that for any graph H, an r-capped recursive decomposition_ R_<sub>H</sub> of H with roots H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>, and for any i, maintains the DDGs of all pieces in the tree rooted at H<sub>i</sub>, with preprocessing time T<sub>pre</sub>(r), handles each edge weight increase affecting H<sub>i</sub> in amortized update time T<sub>u</sub>(r_) _and has query time T<sub>q</sub>(r)._

_Then, there exists an_ online _data structure_ F_, that given a dynamic graph G, an r-division_ \(G_1,G_2,\dots,G_{k^\prime}\)_, maintains the DDG of each piece G<sub>j</sub> with pre-processing time_ \(\tilde{O}(T_{pre}(r))\) _and amortized update time_ \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T_{pre}(r)}\cdot T_q(r)\cdot\sqrt{r}+T_u(r))\) _and query time_ \(\tilde{O}(T_q(r))\).

The proof of the above theorem is rather straight-forward: for a fixed piece _P=G<sub>j</sub>_, we initiate a decremental data structure D on _P_ and then rebuild every \(\Delta\) updates to _P_, the entire data structure D on _P_.

For convenience, at any time step, let us define B to be the batch of insertions that were applied to _P_ since the last time that D was rebuild. Then, at each time step, if an edge weight increase was issued by the adversary, the update is forwarded to D. Independently of the type of update, we can then use the current DDGs of D and the batch B as inputs to the algorithm in Theorem 5.1 to obtain a DDGs of the current graph _H_.

It is easy to convince oneself of correctness. The running time consists of \(T_{pre}(r)/\Delta\) amortized time to rebuild the data structure D, each update to D is processed in time _T<sub>u</sub>(r_) and finally, Theorem 5.1 with the guarantee that B never exceeds size \(\Delta\) (since we rebuild the data structure and reset B after \(\Delta\) updates) ensures that the final DDG data structure that can be queried is created in time \(\tilde{O}(\Delta\cdot\sqrt{r}T_q(r))\) and query time \(\tilde{O}(T_q(r))\). By choice of \(\Delta=\sqrt{\frac{T_{pre}(r)}{T_q(r)\cdot\sqrt{r}}}\), we obtain the stated amortized update time.

## E Dynamic max flow

In this section, we prove Corollary 2.4. We assume that the reader is familiar with the details of \[20\]. It is useful to separate the running time of their data structure into two parts: \(\tilde{O}(n/\sqrt{r}+r)\) worst-case and \(\tilde{O}(n/\sqrt{r})\) amortized time. We focus on each part separately.

The \(\tilde{O}(n/\sqrt{r})\) amortized bound comes from the data structure having to recompute the _r_- division every \(\sqrt{r}\) updates. This recomputation is necessary since \[20\] supports edge insertions and deletions and an inserted edge might have endpoints in distinct pieces, violating the properties of an _r_-division. The way this is handled is to regard each such edge as a trivial piece consisting of only that edge. The issue then is that the number of pieces and the number of boundary vertices of a piece may grow over time. However, by recomputing every \(\sqrt{r}\) updates, the properties of the _r_-division are maintained. Since we only allow edge weight changes, this issue cannot arise so we can immediately eliminate the amortized time bound.

The \(\tilde{O}(n/\sqrt{r}+r)\) worst-case bound is the time it takes to

1. recompute the DDG of the piece containing the edge whose weight was changed,<tbc>

2. recompute candidate min _st_-separating cycles fully contained in that piece, and<tbc>

3. running the coarse version of Reif on the set of boundary vertices of the _r_-division.<tbc>

The first part is immediately improved from \(\tilde{O}(r)\) to \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{r})\) using our new data structure. The second part can be solved by having a recursive max flow/min _st_-cut data structure for each piece. The final part remains unchanged and runs in time \(\tilde{O}(n/\sqrt{r})\) using FR-Dijkstra. We thus get the following recurrence for the improved worst-case time: \(T(n)=\tilde{O}(n/\sqrt{r}+\sqrt{r})+T(r)\). Picking _r_ to be a constant factor smaller than _n_, we get the desired \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})\) worst-case bound from a geometric sums argument.
